sections.title: The big question Linear Programming answers

board_events.text: Linear Programming: the best outcome from limited resources
A Diwali halwai shop makes two sweets: kaju katli and besan laddoo.
Limited khoya, limited sugar, limited hours at the stove.
How many kilos of each should I make so profit is as large as possible?
That single question IS Linear Programming.
LP = the maths of squeezing the best outcome — most profit, least cost — out of limited resources.

board_events.text: Every tool in this chapter exists to answer that one question systematically.

segments.text: <curious>Let me open with a question that sounds simple but is surprisingly hard to eyeball. Here is the setup.
Picture a small halwai shop in the week before Diwali. You can make two sweets, kaju katli and besan laddoo, and each earns a different profit per kilogram.
But you are short on everything that matters: only so much khoya, only so much sugar, and only so many hours at the stove before the festival rush hits.
So here is the question that keeps the shopkeeper up at night. Given everything I am short on, exactly how many kilos of each sweet should I make so that my profit is as large as possible?
That question, in one sentence, is the whole of Linear Programming.
Linear Programming is the mathematics of squeezing the best possible outcome out of limited resources, whether that means the most profit or the least cost.
Think of it as a machine. Limited inputs go in on the left, and we want the single best outcome to come out on the right.
Every tool we build in this chapter exists to answer that one question in a reliable, repeatable way.
<curious>एक सवाल से शुरू करते हैं जो सुनने में simple है लेकिन आँख से अंदाज़ा लगाना मुश्किल है। setup देखिए।
सोचिए एक छोटी सी halwai shop, Diwali से ठीक पहले। आप दो sweets बना सकते हैं, kaju katli और besan laddoo, और हर एक का profit per kilogram अलग है।
लेकिन हर ज़रूरी चीज़ कम है। सिर्फ़ इतना khoya, इतनी sugar, और stove पर इतने ही घंटे festival की भीड़ से पहले।
तो सवाल यह है। जो कुछ कम है उसे देखते हुए, मुझे हर sweet के कितने kilos बनाने चाहिए ताकि मेरा profit ज़्यादा से ज़्यादा हो?
यही एक सवाल, एक line में, पूरा Linear Programming है।
Linear Programming का मतलब है limited resources से best possible outcome निकालने की mathematics, चाहे वो सबसे ज़्यादा profit हो या सबसे कम cost।
इसे एक machine की तरह सोचिए। limited inputs बाईं तरफ़ अंदर जाते हैं, और हम चाहते हैं कि सबसे best outcome दाईं तरफ़ बाहर आए।
इस chapter का हर tool इसी एक सवाल को reliable तरीके से answer करने के लिए बना है।

sections.title: The three building blocks of every LPP

board_events.text: Three ideas do all the work
1. The objective function — the quantity you push to its best value: profit or cost.
'Linear' means $x$ and $y$ appear only to the first power — no $x^2$, no $xy$.
2. The constraints — the limits life puts on you, each a linear inequality.
Only 8 kg khoya, only 12 stove-hours, and you cannot make a negative number of laddoos.
3. The feasible region — every $(x, y)$ pair that respects all the limits at once.
Your answer is guaranteed to live inside the feasible region, or on its edge.

segments.text: Once you strip away the story, every Linear Programming problem is built from just three ideas. Here they are.
First, the objective function. This is the one quantity you want to push to its best value, usually your total profit that you push up, or your total cost that you push down.
We write it as Z equals a x plus b y. Z is the value we optimise, x and y are the quantities we choose, and a and b are the profit or cost per unit.
The word linear is load-bearing. It means x and y appear only to the first power. No x squared, no x times y. That straightness is exactly what makes the method work.
Second, the constraints. These are the limits life puts on you, and each one becomes a linear inequality.
For example, only eight kilograms of khoya, only twelve hours at the stove, and the obvious fact that you cannot make a negative number of laddoos.
Third, the feasible region. This is the set of every x, y pair that respects all the limits at the same time. Plot them and they fill a region of the graph.
<excited>And here is the promise that makes the whole chapter work. Your best answer is guaranteed to live inside that feasible region, or on its edge, never outside it.
story हटा दें तो हर Linear Programming problem सिर्फ़ तीन ideas से बनी होती है। ये रहीं।
पहला, objective function। यह वो एक quantity है जिसे आप best value तक ले जाना चाहते हैं, आम तौर पर total profit जिसे ऊपर, या total cost जिसे नीचे ले जाते हैं।
इसे लिखते हैं Z equals a x plus b y। Z वो value है जिसे optimise करते हैं, x और y वो quantities हैं जो हम choose करते हैं, और a और b हैं profit या cost per unit।
<curious>यहाँ linear शब्द बहुत important है। इसका मतलब x और y सिर्फ़ first power में आते हैं। ना x square, ना x into y। यही सीधापन method को काम करने लायक बनाता है।
दूसरा, constraints। ये वो limits हैं जो ज़िंदगी आप पर लगाती है, और हर एक limit एक linear inequality बन जाती है।
जैसे, सिर्फ़ आठ kilograms khoya, सिर्फ़ बारह घंटे stove पर, और यह obvious बात कि आप negative laddoos नहीं बना सकते।
तीसरा, feasible region। यह हर उस x, y pair का set है जो सारी limits को एक साथ मानता है। इन्हें plot करें तो ये graph का एक region भर देते हैं।
और यही वो promise है जो पूरे chapter को काम करने लायक बनाता है। आपका best answer उसी feasible region के अंदर, या उसके edge पर मिलना guaranteed है, कभी बाहर नहीं।

sections.title: The corner-point intuition and its three caveats

board_events.text: Why the optimum always sits at a corner
Picture the feasible region as a fenced field and $Z = ax + by$ as a ruler reading higher toward the north-east.
You want to stand where the ruler reads highest.

board_events.text: The best spot is NEVER in the open middle — it pokes out at a corner.
So you never search the whole field — you just check the corners.
Caveat 1: an unbounded field may have no maximum — you could keep walking and keep gaining.
Caveat 2: if the ruler lies parallel to a fence, a whole edge ties for best — infinitely many optima.
Caveat 3: the graphical method needs exactly two decision variables — two products, two foods.

segments.text: Now the single most beautiful fact in this chapter, and the reason it is so easy. Let me give you the picture first.
Picture the feasible region as a fenced field. And picture the objective, Z equals a x plus b y, as a ruler whose reading climbs as you walk in one fixed direction, say towards the north-east.
Your job is simple to state. Stand at the spot in the field where the ruler reads highest.
Look at the field on the board. As we slide that ruler outward, the last point it touches before leaving the field is one of the corners.
Here is the key fact. For a straight-line ruler over a field with straight fences, the highest reading is never in the open middle of the field. It always pokes out at a corner.
That is what makes Linear Programming easy. You do not search the whole field. You just check the corners and pick the best one.
But three caveats keep you honest. First, if the field stretches off to infinity, a maximum might not exist at all, because you could keep walking north-east and keep gaining.
Second, if the ruler happens to line up parallel to one fence, then every point along that fence reads the same best value. There are then infinitely many optimal solutions.
Third, this graphical picture only works in two dimensions, that is, two decision variables. With three or more you would need algebra, the simplex method, which is beyond this chapter.
अब इस chapter का सबसे खूबसूरत fact, और यही वजह है कि यह इतना आसान है। पहले picture देखिए।
feasible region को एक बाड़ वाले field की तरह सोचिए। और objective, Z equals a x plus b y, को एक ruler की तरह जिसका reading एक fixed direction में चलने पर बढ़ता है, मान लीजिए north-east की तरफ़।
आपका काम कहने में simple है। field में उस जगह खड़े हो जाइए जहाँ ruler का reading सबसे ऊँचा हो।
board पर field देखिए। जैसे-जैसे हम ruler को बाहर slide करते हैं, field छोड़ने से पहले वो आख़िरी जो point छूता है, वो किसी corner पर होता है।
<excited>यही key fact है। सीधी line वाले ruler और सीधी बाड़ वाले field के लिए, सबसे ऊँचा reading कभी field के खुले बीच में नहीं होता। वो हमेशा किसी corner पर बाहर निकला होता है।
यही Linear Programming को आसान बनाता है। आप पूरा field नहीं ढूँढते। बस corners check करते हैं और सबसे best चुन लेते हैं।
लेकिन तीन caveats आपको honest रखते हैं। पहला, अगर field infinity तक फैला है, तो maximum शायद exist ही ना करे, क्योंकि आप north-east चलते रह सकते हैं और gain करते रह सकते हैं।
दूसरा, अगर ruler किसी एक बाड़ के parallel हो जाए, तो उस बाड़ के हर point का reading एक जैसा best होता है। तब infinitely many optimal solutions होते हैं।
तीसरा, यह graphical picture सिर्फ़ two dimensions में चलती है, यानी दो decision variables। तीन या ज़्यादा के लिए algebra चाहिए, simplex method, जो इस chapter के बाहर है।

sections.title: Key definitions and two must-know properties

board_events.text: The vocabulary examiners expect, verbatim
Objective function: the quantity being optimised, $Z = ax + by$.
Decision variables $x, y$: the quantities you choose. Constants $a, b$: profit or cost per unit.
Feasible region: the common region satisfying ALL constraints, including non-negativity $x \ge 0,\ y \ge 0$.
Bounded region: fits inside a circle. Unbounded region: extends to infinity in some direction.
Corner point (vertex): a point formed where two boundary lines intersect.
Feasible solution = any point in/on the region. Optimal solution = the feasible point giving the best $Z$.
Property 1: a bounded feasible region for a linear objective is a convex polygon — no dents.
Property 2: equal optimum at two corners ⇒ the same value at every point on the joining segment.

segments.text: Linear Programming has no SI units and no dimensional formulae, because it is a method. So the key facts here are precise definitions, and examiners want these exact words.
The objective function is the quantity being optimised, written Z equals a x plus b y.
The decision variables x and y are the quantities you get to choose. The constants a and b are the profit or cost per unit, usually positive numbers.

The feasible region is the common region that satisfies all the constraints at once, and that includes the non-negativity conditions x greater than or equal to zero and y greater than or equal to zero.
A bounded region is one you can enclose inside a circle. An unbounded region extends to infinity in some direction.
A corner point, also called a vertex, is a point formed where two boundary lines intersect.
Keep two more straight. A feasible solution is any point inside or on the boundary of the region. An optimal solution is the feasible point that gives the best value of Z.

Now two properties worth memorising. First, a bounded feasible region for a linear objective is always a convex polygon, with no dents, so a straight line joining any two feasible points stays entirely inside.
Second, if Z takes the same optimum value at two corner points, then it takes that same value at every point on the segment joining them. That is the seed of multiple optimal solutions.
Linear Programming में ना कोई S I units हैं ना dimensional formulae, क्योंकि यह एक method है। तो यहाँ key facts हैं precise definitions, और examiners यही exact शब्द चाहते हैं।
objective function वो quantity है जिसे optimise किया जाता है, लिखते हैं Z equals a x plus b y।
decision variables x और y वो quantities हैं जो आप choose करते हैं। constants a और b हैं profit या cost per unit, आम तौर पर positive numbers।
feasible region वो common region है जो सारी constraints को एक साथ satisfy करता है, और इसमें non-negativity conditions x greater than or equal to zero और y greater than or equal to zero शामिल हैं।
bounded region वो है जिसे आप एक circle के अंदर बंद कर सकें। unbounded region किसी direction में infinity तक फैलता है।
corner point, जिसे vertex भी कहते हैं, वो point है जहाँ दो boundary lines एक दूसरे को काटती हैं।
दो और terms साफ़ रखिए। feasible solution region के अंदर या boundary पर कोई भी point है। optimal solution वो feasible point है जो Z की best value देता है।

अब दो properties याद रखने लायक। पहली, linear objective के लिए bounded feasible region हमेशा एक convex polygon होता है, बिना किसी dent के, तो किन्हीं दो feasible points को जोड़ने वाली सीधी line पूरी तरह अंदर रहती है।
दूसरी, अगर Z दो corner points पर एक ही optimum value लेता है, तो वो उन्हें जोड़ने वाले segment के हर point पर वही value लेता है। यही multiple optimal solutions की जड़ है।

segments.text: The whole method rests on two theorems. C B S E states them and does not ask for a formal proof, so know them precisely, and know the procedure they justify.
Theorem one, the most important line in the chapter. When Z has an optimal value, that optimum lives at a corner.
Formally, let R be the feasible region and Z equals a x plus b y the objective. Whenever Z has an optimal value, maximum or minimum, over R, that value must occur at a corner point, a vertex of R.
The picture on the board shows why. We slide the objective line across the region, and watch where it leaves.

As you slide the line a x plus b y equals k outward, the last feasible point it touches before leaving is always a vertex, unless the line is parallel to an edge, in which case it leaves along a whole edge whose endpoints are still vertices.
Theorem two handles the shape of the region.
If the region is bounded, then Z is guaranteed to have both a maximum and a minimum, and each of them occurs at a corner point. Nothing can go wrong.
If the region is unbounded, a maximum or a minimum may or may not exist. But if it does exist, it still occurs at a corner point.

sections.title: The corner-point method

board_events.text: The corner-point method, step by step
Step 1 — Draw the feasible region: turn each inequality into its boundary line and shade the correct side.
Origin test: plug in $(0, 0)$. If it satisfies the inequality, shade the origin's side.
Step 2 — Find every corner point where boundary lines cross (solve the two line equations together).
Step 3 — Evaluate $Z$ at every corner. Record the largest value $M$ and the smallest value $m$.
Step 4, bounded region: $M$ is the maximum and $m$ is the minimum. Done.
Step 4, unbounded region: you MUST verify with a half-plane test before writing the answer.
Max $M$ genuine only if $ax + by \gt M$ misses the region; min $m$ only if $ax + by \lt m$ misses it.

segments.text: Those two theorems justify one clean procedure, the corner-point method. Four steps, and step four has a fork.
Step one, draw the feasible region. Convert each inequality into its boundary line by replacing the inequality sign with an equals sign, plot the line, and shade the correct side.

To pick the correct side, use the origin test. Substitute the point zero, zero into the inequality. If it holds, shade the side containing the origin. If it fails, shade the other side. Use a different test point only if the line passes through the origin.
Step two, find all the corner points. These are the vertices where boundary lines cross. Read them off by inspection, or solve the two intersecting line equations simultaneously.
Step three, evaluate Z at every single corner point. Build a small table of corner point against value of Z, and mark the largest value big M and the smallest value small m.
Step four now forks on the shape. If the region is bounded, you are done. Big M is the maximum and small m is the minimum.
But if the region is unbounded, you must not stop yet. You have to verify with a half-plane test before writing any answer.

The test is this. Big M is the genuine maximum only if the open half-plane a x plus b y greater than big M has no point in common with the region. Likewise small m is the true minimum only if a x plus b y less than small m misses the region.
ये दो theorems एक साफ़ procedure justify करते हैं, corner-point method। चार steps, और step four में एक fork है।
step one, feasible region draw करें। हर inequality को उसकी boundary line में बदलें, यानी inequality sign की जगह equals sign, line plot करें, और सही side shade करें।

सही side चुनने के लिए origin test इस्तेमाल करें। point zero, zero को inequality में डालिए। अगर सही बैठे, तो origin वाली side shade करें। अगर नहीं, तो दूसरी side। अलग test point तभी लें जब line origin से गुज़रती हो।
step two, सारे corner points ढूँढें। ये वो vertices हैं जहाँ boundary lines cross करती हैं। inspection से पढ़ लें, या दोनों lines के equations एक साथ solve करें।
step three, Z को हर एक corner point पर evaluate करें। corner point बनाम Z की value की एक छोटी table बनाएँ, और सबसे बड़ी value को big M और सबसे छोटी को small m mark करें।
step four अब shape पर fork करता है। अगर region bounded है, तो काम ख़त्म। big M maximum है और small m minimum।

segments.text: Let me consolidate the forms you will write again and again. Treat this section as a reference card you can jump straight to.
The heart of every problem is the objective function, Z equals a x plus b y.
First, the standard maximisation problem. This is the profit family, where your resources act as upper limits.

You write, maximise Z equals a x plus b y, subject to c one x plus d one y less than or equal to e one, c two x plus d two y less than or equal to e two, and so on, together with x and y both greater than or equal to zero.
Second, the standard minimisation problem. This is the cost family, where requirements act as lower limits.
You write, minimise Z equals a x plus b y, subject to constraints of the greater-than-or-equal type, again with x and y both greater than or equal to zero.
Now the two verification tests for unbounded regions, the lines that earn marks. For a maximum, ask whether the open half-plane beats your best corner.
If a x plus b y greater than big M shares any point with the region, then no maximum exists. Otherwise big M is the genuine maximum.
For a minimum, ask the mirror question about beating your smallest corner value.
If a x plus b y less than small m shares any point with the region, then no minimum exists. Otherwise small m is the genuine minimum.

segments.text: Here is a fast C U E T style question that hides a trap. The corner points of a feasible region are given as zero comma four, three comma three, and six comma zero, and the objective is Z equals two x plus two y.
No graph is needed. We just read the given corners.
Evaluate at each. At zero comma four Z is eight. At three comma three Z is twelve. At six comma zero Z is also twelve.
Notice what happened. The maximum value twelve is reached at two corners at once, three comma three and six comma zero.
The picture explains it. The objective line for Z equals twelve runs exactly parallel to the edge joining those two corners.
So by the multiple-optima property, when Z hits the same optimum at two corners, every point on the segment joining them is also optimal.
That means the answer is not a single corner. It is the whole edge between three comma three and six comma zero, an infinite set of optimal points.
The speed tip to carry away. The moment two corner values tie for the optimum, stop computing. Your answer is the entire edge between them, and the objective line is parallel to that edge.

कोई graph नहीं चाहिए। हम बस दिए गए corners पढ़ते हैं।
हर एक पर evaluate करें। zero comma four पर Z है eight। three comma three पर Z है twelve। six comma zero पर Z भी twelve।
ग़ौर कीजिए क्या हुआ। maximum value twelve एक साथ दो corners पर पहुँचती है, three comma three और six comma zero।
picture इसे समझाती है। Z equals twelve की objective line ठीक उन दोनों corners को जोड़ने वाले edge के parallel चलती है।
तो multiple-optima property से, जब Z दो corners पर एक ही optimum छूता है, तो उन्हें जोड़ने वाले segment का हर point भी optimal होता है।
इसका मतलब answer एक अकेला corner नहीं है। यह three comma three और six comma zero के बीच का पूरा edge है, optimal points का infinite set।
साथ ले जाने वाली speed tip। जिस पल दो corner values optimum के लिए tie करें, calculate करना रोक दीजिए। आपका answer उनके बीच का पूरा edge है, और objective line उस edge के parallel है।

segments.text: Now the case examiners love, an unbounded region with a real minimum. A dairy farmer mixes two feeds, P and Q, in kilograms, to feed the herd cheaply.
Each kilogram of P supplies one unit of protein and two units of fibre. Each kilogram of Q supplies one unit of protein and one unit of fibre.
The herd needs at least six units of protein and at least eight units of fibre daily. Feed P costs five rupees a kilogram and Feed Q costs four rupees a kilogram.
This is a cost problem, so we minimise. Z equals five x plus four y.
The requirements use greater-than-or-equal signs. x plus y greater than or equal to six for protein, two x plus y greater than or equal to eight for fibre, with x and y non-negative.
Because both constraints are greater-than-or-equal, the region lies above both lines and stretches to infinity. It is unbounded, as the up-right arrow shows.

Find the boundary corners. The lines cross at two comma four. So the corner points are zero comma eight giving thirty two, two comma four giving twenty six, and six comma zero giving thirty. The smallest is twenty six.

But the region is unbounded, so we must verify. Does five x plus four y less than twenty six meet the region? The line five x plus four y equals twenty six touches the region only at two comma four, and moving into the region up and to the right only increases the cost. No feasible point beats twenty six.
So the minimum cost is twenty six rupees, achieved with two kilograms of Feed P and four kilograms of Feed Q. That verification line is exactly what earns the marks.

P के हर kilogram से एक unit protein और दो units fibre मिलते हैं। Q के हर kilogram से एक unit protein और एक unit fibre।
herd को रोज़ कम से कम छह units protein और कम से कम आठ units fibre चाहिए। Feed P की cost पाँच rupees per kilogram और Feed Q की चार rupees per kilogram।
यह cost problem है, तो हम minimise करते हैं। Z equals five x plus four y।

requirements greater-than-or-equal signs इस्तेमाल करती हैं। x plus y greater than or equal to six protein के लिए, two x plus y greater than or equal to eight fibre के लिए, साथ में x और y non-negative।
क्योंकि दोनों constraints greater-than-or-equal हैं, region दोनों lines के ऊपर है और infinity तक फैला है। यह unbounded है, जैसा up-right arrow दिखाता है।

boundary corners ढूँढें। lines two comma four पर cross करती हैं। तो corner points हैं zero comma eight जो thirty two देता है, two comma four जो twenty six देता है, और six comma zero जो thirty। सबसे छोटा है twenty six।

लेकिन region unbounded है, तो verify करना ज़रूरी है। क्या five x plus four y less than twenty six region से मिलता है? line five x plus four y equals twenty six region को सिर्फ़ two comma four पर छूती है, और region के अंदर ऊपर-दाएँ जाने से cost सिर्फ़ बढ़ती है। कोई feasible point twenty six को beat नहीं करता।
तो minimum cost है twenty six rupees, जो दो kilograms Feed P और चार kilograms Feed Q से मिलती है। वही verification line marks दिलाती है।

sections.title: Finding the condition for a maximum shared across an edge

board_events.text: Worked example — the condition for a shared maximum
Corner points (0, 5), (2, 3), (5, 0). Objective $Z = px + qy$ with $p, q \gt 0$.
We want the maximum shared by (2, 3) and (5, 0): set $Z(2,3) = Z(5,0)$.
Geometric check: the edge from (2, 3) to (5, 0) has slope $-1$.

board_events.latex: \text{slope of } px + qy = c \ \text{ is } \ -\frac{p}{q} = -1 \;\Rightarrow\; p = q

board_events.text: Optimum spreads along a whole edge exactly when the objective line is parallel to it.
Condition: $p = q$.

segments.text: One more reasoning-level question, running the tie idea backwards. The corner points are zero comma five, two comma three, and five comma zero, and the objective is Z equals p x plus q y with p and q positive.
We are asked for the condition on p and q so that the maximum is shared by two corners, namely two comma three and five comma zero.
For a shared maximum, Z must take equal values at those two corners. So we set Z at two comma three equal to Z at five comma zero.
That gives two p plus three q equals five p. Cancel and three q equals three p, so p equals q.
Let me confirm this geometrically, which is the deeper reason. The edge joining two comma three and five comma zero has slope zero minus three over five minus two, that is minus one.

The objective line p x plus q y equals c has slope minus p over q. The optimum spreads across a whole edge exactly when the objective line is parallel to that edge, so minus p over q equals minus one, giving p equals q again.
So the algebra and the geometry agree, and this is the general principle. An optimum stretches along an entire edge precisely when the objective line is parallel to that edge.
The condition asked for is simply p equals q.
एक और reasoning-level सवाल, tie वाले idea को उल्टा चलाते हुए। corner points हैं zero comma five, two comma three, और five comma zero, और objective है Z equals p x plus q y जिसमें p और q positive हैं।
हमसे p और q पर condition पूछी गई है ताकि maximum दो corners पर share हो, यानी two comma three और five comma zero पर।
shared maximum के लिए, Z को उन दोनों corners पर बराबर values लेनी होंगी। तो हम Z at two comma three को Z at five comma zero के बराबर रखते हैं।
इससे मिलता है two p plus three q equals five p। cancel करें तो three q equals three p, यानी p equals q।
इसे geometrically confirm करता हूँ, जो गहरी वजह है। two comma three और five comma zero को जोड़ने वाले edge का slope है zero minus three बटा five minus two, यानी minus one।
objective line p x plus q y equals c का slope है minus p over q। optimum पूरे edge पर तभी फैलता है जब objective line उस edge के parallel हो, तो minus p over q equals minus one, जिससे फिर p equals q।
तो algebra और geometry दोनों सहमत हैं, और यही general principle है। optimum पूरे edge पर ठीक तब फैलता है जब objective line उस edge के parallel हो।
पूछी गई condition बस इतनी है, p equals q।

sections.title: Common pitfalls and a time-saving pro-tip

board_events.text: Where marks are won and lost
Pitfall 1 — stopping at the axis corners and missing the interior vertex where two slanted constraints cross.
The optimum very often hides at that interior vertex — always list EVERY corner.
Pitfall 2 — forgetting the unbounded check. Examiners specifically look for the half-plane verification line.
Pitfall 3 — shading the wrong side. Confusing ≤ and ≥ flips your entire region.
Use the origin test every time: if $(0, 0)$ fits the inequality, shade its side.
Pitfall 4 — mixing up 'at most' (≤) and 'at least' (≥). One wrong word changes the answer entirely.
Pro-tip: in cost minimisation, evaluate the interior vertex where two ≥ constraints meet first.

segments.text: Let me close Part one with the four places students actually lose marks here, and the pro-tip that saves time.
Pitfall one, stopping at the axis corners. Many students evaluate Z only at the intercepts, the points on the x-axis and y-axis, and miss the interior vertex where two slanted constraints cross.
That interior vertex is very often exactly where the optimum hides, as it did in both the bakery and the dairy problems. So always list every single corner before you decide.

Pitfall two, forgetting the unbounded check. Reading off the smallest or largest corner value and writing answer, without the half-plane verification, costs you the marks in an unbounded problem. Examiners look for that verification line specifically.
Pitfall three, shading the wrong side. Confusing less-than-or-equal with greater-than-or-equal flips your entire region, and every corner after that is wrong.
The fix is mechanical. Use the origin test every single time. Plug in zero, zero. If the inequality holds, shade the side containing the origin. If not, shade the other side.

Pitfall four, mixing up at most and at least. At most three hundred means less than or equal to three hundred. At least six units means greater than or equal to six. A single mistranslated word changes a maximisation answer entirely, so underline these words while formulating.
And the pro-tip to save time. For cost minimisation problems, the optimum almost always sits at the interior vertex where two greater-than-or-equal constraints intersect, so evaluate that one first.
Part one को उन चार जगहों से बंद करते हैं जहाँ students सचमुच marks खोते हैं, और उस pro-tip से जो time बचाती है।

pitfall one, axis corners पर रुक जाना। कई students Z को सिर्फ़ intercepts पर evaluate करते हैं, यानी x-axis और y-axis वाले points पर, और वो interior vertex miss कर देते हैं जहाँ दो slanted constraints cross करती हैं।
वही interior vertex अक्सर ठीक वो जगह होती है जहाँ optimum छिपा होता है, जैसा bakery और dairy दोनों में हुआ। तो decide करने से पहले हमेशा हर एक corner list कीजिए।

pitfall two, unbounded check भूल जाना। सबसे छोटी या बड़ी corner value पढ़कर answer लिख देना, बिना half-plane verification के, unbounded problem में marks का नुक़सान करता है। examiners वही verification line ख़ास तौर पर ढूँढते हैं।
pitfall three, ग़लत side shade करना। less-than-or-equal और greater-than-or-equal को confuse करना पूरा region उलट देता है, और उसके बाद हर corner ग़लत हो जाता है।
इसका इलाज mechanical है। हर बार origin test इस्तेमाल कीजिए। zero, zero डालिए। अगर inequality सही बैठे, तो origin वाली side shade करें। नहीं तो दूसरी side।

pitfall four, at most और at least को मिला देना। at most three hundred का मतलब less than or equal to three hundred। at least six units का मतलब greater than or equal to six। एक ग़लत translate हुआ शब्द पूरा maximisation answer बदल देता है, तो formulate करते समय इन शब्दों को underline कीजिए।
और time बचाने वाली pro-tip। cost minimisation problems में optimum लगभग हमेशा उस interior vertex पर होता है जहाँ दो greater-than-or-equal constraints मिलती हैं, तो सबसे पहले उसी को evaluate कीजिए।

sections.title: Formulation is translating words into mathematics

board_events.text: Formulation: turning a paragraph into mathematics
In an exam nobody hands you the inequalities — they hand you a paragraph.
Opener: 'A tailoring unit has 40 metres of cloth and 18 hours of machine time…'
The hardest, most marks-rich skill here is turning those words into a model.
Think of yourself as a translator at a railway enquiry counter.
The passenger speaks everyday language; you convert it into the system's exact codes.
'We can't afford more than ₹5000' becomes the exact symbol: cost ≤ 5000.
Get one word wrong — 'at least' read as 'at most' — and the whole answer collapses.

segments.text: In Subtopic one you learned how to solve a Linear Programming problem once it is written in clean mathematical form. Now we tackle the harder half.
Because in a real exam, and in real life, nobody hands you the inequalities ready-made. They hand you a paragraph of ordinary language.
Something like, a tailoring unit has forty metres of cloth and eighteen hours of machine time, and so on. Your first job is to convert that story into mathematics.
That conversion is called formulation, and it is the hardest and most marks-rich skill in this whole chapter. Get it right and everything after is mechanical.
Here is the mindset. Think of yourself as a translator sitting at a railway enquiry counter.
A passenger speaks to you in everyday Hindi or Tamil, and you must convert their request into the precise codes the booking system understands.
Formulation is exactly that translation. The loose sentence, we cannot afford more than five thousand rupees, becomes the exact symbol, cost less than or equal to five thousand.
And here is the warning that runs through this subtopic. Get one single word wrong, read at least as at most, and the entire answer collapses, no matter how perfectly you draw the graph afterwards.
Subtopic one में आपने सीखा कि एक Linear Programming problem को clean mathematical form में लिखने के बाद कैसे solve करते हैं। अब हम मुश्किल आधा हिस्सा लेते हैं।
क्योंकि असली exam में, और असल ज़िंदगी में, कोई आपको inequalities बनी-बनाई नहीं देता। वो आपको एक paragraph देते हैं, आम भाषा में।
जैसे, एक tailoring unit के पास चालीस metres cloth और अठारह घंटे machine time है, वग़ैरह। आपका पहला काम है उस कहानी को mathematics में बदलना।
इस बदलाव को formulation कहते हैं, और यही इस पूरे chapter का सबसे मुश्किल और सबसे ज़्यादा marks वाला skill है। इसे सही कर लिया तो बाकी सब mechanical है।
mindset यह है। खुद को railway enquiry counter पर बैठा एक translator समझिए।
एक passenger आपसे रोज़मर्रा की Hindi या Tamil में बात करता है, और आपको उसकी request को उन precise codes में बदलना है जो booking system समझता है।
formulation ठीक वही translation है। ढीला वाक्य, हम पाँच हज़ार rupees से ज़्यादा afford नहीं कर सकते, बन जाता है exact symbol, cost less than or equal to five thousand।
<whisper>और यही warning इस पूरे subtopic में चलती है। एक भी शब्द ग़लत कर दिया, at least को at most पढ़ लिया, तो पूरा answer गिर जाता है, चाहे आप बाद में graph कितना ही perfect बना लें।

sections.title: The three questions every LPP word problem asks

board_events.text: Every word problem asks the same three questions
1. What am I choosing? → the decision variables $x$ and $y$, with units.
How many tables? how many hectares? how many scoops?
2. What am I trying to make best? → the objective $Z = ax + by$.
Total profit to push up, or total cost to push down.
3. What's stopping me? → each limit becomes a constraint, a linear inequality.
Material, money, time, demand, a promise to a customer — each is one constraint.
Factory production, diet, transport, scheduling — the same skeleton in different costumes.

segments.text: However the problem is dressed up — sweaters or sand, calculators or crops — it is built from the same three questions. Train your eye to hunt for these three things.
Question one, what am I choosing? The unknown quantities you control become the decision variables x and y. Always write their units.
Ask it concretely. How many tables? how many hectares of land? how many scoops of powder? Whatever the problem asks you to decide, that becomes x and y.
Question two, what am I trying to make best? The total profit or total cost you want to push becomes the objective function, Z equals a x plus b y.
If it is profit or output, you push the value up and maximise. If it is cost or time or waste, you push it down and minimise.
Question three, what is stopping me? Every limit in the paragraph becomes a constraint, and each constraint is a linear inequality.
The limit could be material, money, machine time, customer demand, or a promise you made. Each separate limit is one separate constraint.
Once you hunt for these three things, every problem starts to look the same. Factory production, diet planning, transport, scheduling, they are just different costumes on one skeleton.
problem चाहे जैसे भी सजी हो, sweaters हों या sand, calculators हों या crops, वो उन्हीं तीन सवालों से बनी होती है। अपनी नज़र को इन तीन चीज़ों को ढूँढना सिखाइए।
सवाल एक, मैं क्या choose कर रहा हूँ? जो unknown quantities आप control करते हैं वो बन जाती हैं decision variables x और y। इनकी units हमेशा लिखिए।
इसे ठोस तरीके से पूछिए। कितनी tables? कितने hectares ज़मीन? कितने scoops powder? problem जो भी decide करने को कहे, वही x और y बनता है।
सवाल दो, मैं क्या best करना चाहता हूँ? जो total profit या total cost आप push करना चाहते हैं वो बनता है objective function, Z equals a x plus b y।
अगर profit या output है, तो value ऊपर push करते हैं और maximise। अगर cost या time या waste है, तो नीचे push करते हैं और minimise।
सवाल तीन, मुझे क्या रोक रहा है? paragraph की हर limit एक constraint बनती है, और हर constraint एक linear inequality है।
limit material हो सकती है, money, machine time, customer demand, या कोई promise जो आपने किया। हर अलग limit एक अलग constraint है।
इन तीन चीज़ों को ढूँढना शुरू करते ही हर problem एक जैसी दिखने लगती है। factory production, diet planning, transport, scheduling, ये बस एक skeleton पर अलग-अलग costumes हैं।

sections.title: Four assumptions that make or break the model

board_events.text: Assumptions to watch — when this works, and when it bites
Proportionality: doubling production must exactly double the resource used and the profit.
A bulk discount or setup cost breaks linearity — the corner-point method no longer applies.
Divisibility: the graphical method allows fractional answers like $x = 2.5$.
CBSE problems are usually designed so the optimum lands on whole numbers.
Hidden non-negativity: buses, kilograms, hours can never be negative.
Read EVERY clause: 'type B cannot exceed type A by more than 100' is a whole constraint.
Skip one such sentence and the answer changes entirely.

segments.text: Before we build the procedure, four assumptions decide whether this method even applies. Know them so you can spot when a problem breaks the rules.
First, proportionality. Doubling your production must exactly double the resource you use and the profit you earn. The relationship has to be a straight line.
So watch out. If there is a bulk discount, or a one-time setup cost, the objective stops being a straight line, and the whole corner-point method no longer applies.
Second, divisibility. The graphical method happily allows fractional answers, such as x equals two point five.
In real life you cannot make half a sweater, so we round sensibly. And thankfully, C B S E problems are usually designed so the optimum lands neatly on whole numbers.
Third, hidden non-negativity. Number of buses, kilograms of fertiliser, hours worked, none of these can ever be negative.
And fourth, the big one. Read every single clause. A sentence like, type B cannot exceed type A by more than one hundred, is an entire constraint hiding in plain English.
Skip one such sentence and the answer changes entirely. In this subtopic, missing a clause is the classic way to lose marks.
procedure बनाने से पहले, चार assumptions तय करती हैं कि यह method apply भी होता है या नहीं। इन्हें जानिए ताकि आप पहचान सकें कब कोई problem नियम तोड़ रही है।
पहला, proportionality। आपकी production double करने से जो resource आप use करते हैं और जो profit कमाते हैं वो बिल्कुल double होना चाहिए। रिश्ता एक सीधी line होना चाहिए।
तो सावधान। अगर कोई bulk discount है, या एक बार का setup cost, तो objective सीधी line नहीं रहता, और पूरा corner-point method apply नहीं होता।
दूसरा, divisibility। graphical method ख़ुशी से fractional answers allow करता है, जैसे x equals two point five।
असल ज़िंदगी में आप आधा sweater नहीं बना सकते, तो हम समझदारी से round करते हैं। और शुक्र है, C B S E problems अक्सर ऐसी बनी होती हैं कि optimum ठीक whole numbers पर आ जाए।
तीसरा, hidden non-negativity। number of buses, kilograms fertiliser, hours worked, इनमें से कोई भी कभी negative नहीं हो सकता।
और चौथा, सबसे बड़ा। हर एक clause पढ़िए। एक वाक्य जैसे, type B, type A से सौ से ज़्यादा नहीं बढ़ सकता, एक पूरा constraint है जो सीधे English में छिपा है।
ऐसा एक वाक्य छोड़ दिया तो answer पूरी तरह बदल जाता है। इस subtopic में, एक clause miss करना marks खोने का classic तरीका है।

sections.title: The constraint-type dictionary and model anatomy

board_events.text: The constraint-type dictionary — translate the English
'at most', 'no more than', 'cannot exceed', 'available', 'within' → upper limit → ≤
'at least', 'minimum of', 'no less than', 'requires' → lower limit → ≥
'exactly', 'must equal', 'all of it is used' → balance → =
'cannot be negative' (items, hours, kg) → non-negativity → $x, y \ge 0$
Anatomy: objective $Z = ax+by$, then structural constraints, then $x \ge 0,\ y \ge 0$.
The goal word usually names the family: 'profit' → maximise; 'cost' → minimise.
Every constraint and the objective share the SAME two decision variables.

segments.text: Here is the dictionary that does the heavy lifting. Learn these word-to-symbol matches cold, because examiners phrase constraints using exactly these signals.
When you see at most, no more than, cannot exceed, available, or within, that is an upper limit on a resource, and it translates to a less-than-or-equal sign.
When you see at least, minimum of, no less than, or requires, that is a lower limit, a requirement, and it translates to a greater-than-or-equal sign.
When you see exactly, must equal, or all of it is used, that is a balance condition, and it becomes an equals sign.
And the phrase cannot be negative, applied to items or hours or kilograms, gives the non-negativity conditions x and y greater than or equal to zero.
Assemble them in this order. First the objective, Z equals a x plus b y. Then the structural constraints. Then, always last, the non-negativity conditions.
The goal word usually tells you the family in advance. The word profit means maximise. The word cost means minimise.

And one property ties it all together. Every constraint and the objective must be written in the same two decision variables. If a quantity cannot be expressed using x and y alone, you chose your variables badly.
यह रहा वो dictionary जो सारा भारी काम करता है। इन word-to-symbol जोड़ियों को पक्का याद कर लीजिए, क्योंकि examiners constraints को ठीक इन्हीं signals से लिखते हैं।
जब आप देखें at most, no more than, cannot exceed, available, या within, तो यह किसी resource पर upper limit है, और यह less-than-or-equal sign में बदलता है।
जब आप देखें at least, minimum of, no less than, या requires, तो यह एक lower limit है, एक requirement, और यह greater-than-or-equal sign में बदलता है।
जब आप देखें exactly, must equal, या all of it is used, तो यह एक balance condition है, और यह equals sign बन जाता है।
और phrase cannot be negative, जो items या hours या kilograms पर लगे, वो देता है non-negativity conditions, x और y greater than or equal to zero।
इन्हें इस order में जमाइए। पहले objective, Z equals a x plus b y। फिर structural constraints। फिर, हमेशा आख़िर में, non-negativity conditions।
goal word अक्सर पहले ही family बता देता है। शब्द profit का मतलब maximise। शब्द cost का मतलब minimise।
और एक property सब कुछ जोड़ती है। हर constraint और objective एक ही दो decision variables में लिखे होने चाहिए। अगर कोई quantity सिर्फ़ x और y से नहीं लिख सकते, तो आपने variables ग़लत चुने।

sections.title: The five-step formulation procedure

board_events.text: The five-step formulation procedure
Step 1 — Name the decision variables, with units: '$x$ = number of cricket bats'.
Step 2 — Write the objective $Z = (\text{rate}_x)\,x + (\text{rate}_y)\,y$; state max or min.
Step 3 — Translate each restriction clause-by-clause into a linear inequality.
Working clause by clause means you never miss a hidden constraint.
Step 4 — Add non-negativity $x \ge 0,\ y \ge 0$ (this also fences the region into quadrant I).
Step 5 — State the complete model: 'Maximise $Z = \dots$ subject to $\dots$'.

board_events.text: Memory hook — N-O-C-N: Name variables, Objective, Constraints, Non-negativity.

segments.text: Formulation is a procedure, not a theorem, so here is the disciplined five-step framework. Follow it in order every time.

Step one, name the decision variables and write their units. For example, let x equal the number of cricket bats and y the number of tennis racquets. Stating units now stops you mixing hours with items later.

Step two, write the objective function. Find the per-unit profit or cost of each variable and combine, Z equals rate for x times x plus rate for y times y. Say clearly whether you maximise or minimise.
Step three, translate each restriction. Go through the paragraph one sentence at a time, and for each limit write a linear inequality using the dictionary to fix the direction of the sign.
Working clause by clause is the whole discipline. It is the only reliable way to make sure no hidden constraint slips past you.
Step four, add non-negativity, x and y greater than or equal to zero. This is physically obvious, and it also fences the whole region into the first quadrant.
Step five, state the complete model together, maximise Z equals something subject to the full list of constraints. A clean, collected model is what earns the formulation marks.
The board shows the journey. A word problem goes through the five-step formulation into an L P P model, then through the corner-point method into the optimal solution.
One memory hook to carry the whole procedure. N O C N. Name the variables, write the Objective, list the Constraints, add Non-negativity.

step one, decision variables को नाम दीजिए और उनकी units लिखिए। जैसे, माना x है cricket bats की संख्या और y है tennis racquets की। units अभी लिखने से आप बाद में hours और items नहीं मिलाएँगे।
step two, objective function लिखिए। हर variable का per-unit profit या cost ढूँढिए और जोड़िए, Z equals rate for x times x plus rate for y times y। साफ़ कहिए कि maximise कर रहे हैं या minimise।
step three, हर restriction translate कीजिए। paragraph को एक-एक वाक्य करके पढ़िए, और हर limit के लिए एक linear inequality लिखिए, dictionary से sign की direction तय करते हुए।

step four, non-negativity जोड़िए, x और y greater than or equal to zero। यह physically obvious है, और यह पूरे region को first quadrant में भी बंद कर देता है।
step five, पूरा model एक साथ लिखिए, maximise Z equals कुछ subject to constraints की पूरी list। एक साफ़, इकट्ठा model ही formulation के marks दिलाता है।
board सफ़र दिखाता है। एक word problem पाँच-step formulation से गुज़रकर L P P model बनता है, फिर corner-point method से गुज़रकर optimal solution।

sections.title: The four application families

board_events.text: The four application families
Manufacturing / product-mix → maximise profit; signature: resources ≤ available.
Diet / nutrition / blending → minimise cost; signature: nutrients ≥ required.
Transportation / allocation → minimise cost; signature: supply ≤, demand ≥.
Scheduling / time → maximise output; signature: time ≤, minimum targets ≥.
Goal word = family: profit/output → maximise, expect ≤; cost/requirement → minimise, expect ≥.
Cost problems often give an unbounded region — the Sub-01 verification step will matter.
Spot the family and you already know the shape of the answer.

segments.text: Almost every problem you will meet belongs to one of four families. Recognise the family on sight and you already know the shape of the whole answer.

Family one, manufacturing or product-mix. A factory makes two products from limited material or machine time. The goal is maximise profit, and its signature is resources less than or equal to what is available.

Family two, diet, nutrition, or blending. You mix two foods or feeds to meet minimum requirements cheaply. The goal is minimise cost, and its signature is nutrients greater than or equal to what is required.

Family three, transportation or allocation. You distribute goods, or split land between two uses. The goal is usually minimise cost, with a mix of supply less-than-or-equal and demand greater-than-or-equal.
Family four, scheduling or time. You divide limited hours between two activities. The goal is maximise output or earnings, with time less-than-or-equal and minimum targets greater-than-or-equal.

The shortcut is the goal word. Profit, output, or distance means maximise, and you expect less-than-or-equal constraints. Cost or requirement means minimise, and you expect greater-than-or-equal constraints.
And here is the connection back to Subtopic one. Those cost problems very often produce an unbounded region, so the half-plane verification step you learned earlier will matter.
So spot the family first. Once you know whether it is a max or a min, and which way the constraints point, half your formulation work is already done.
जो भी problem आपको मिलेगी वो लगभग हमेशा चार families में से एक की होगी। family को देखते ही पहचान लीजिए और आप पूरे answer की shape पहले से जान जाएँगे।
family one, manufacturing या product-mix। एक factory limited material या machine time से दो products बनाती है। goal है maximise profit, और इसकी signature है resources less than or equal to available।

family two, diet, nutrition, या blending। आप दो foods या feeds मिलाते हैं ताकि minimum requirements सस्ते में पूरी हों। goal है minimise cost, और signature है nutrients greater than or equal to required।

family three, transportation या allocation। आप goods बाँटते हैं, या ज़मीन को दो uses में बाँटते हैं। goal आम तौर पर minimise cost, supply less-than-or-equal और demand greater-than-or-equal के mix के साथ।
family four, scheduling या time। आप limited hours को दो activities में बाँटते हैं। goal है maximise output या earnings, time less-than-or-equal और minimum targets greater-than-or-equal के साथ।

shortcut है goal word। profit, output, या distance का मतलब maximise, और आप less-than-or-equal constraints की उम्मीद करें। cost या requirement का मतलब minimise, और greater-than-or-equal constraints की उम्मीद करें।
और यह रहा Subtopic one से connection। वो cost problems अक्सर एक unbounded region बनाती हैं, तो जो half-plane verification step आपने पहले सीखा था वो यहाँ matter करेगा।
तो पहले family पहचानिए। जैसे ही आप जान लें कि यह max है या min, और constraints किस तरफ़ इशारा करती हैं, आपका आधा formulation काम पहले ही हो चुका है।

sections.title: Standard skeleton and the two trap translations

board_events.text: Translation forms — the exact symbols to write
Standard model skeleton:

board_events.latex: \text{Maximise / Minimise } Z = ax + by \ \text{ subject to structural constraints, } \ x \ge 0,\ y \ge 0

board_events.text: Trap 1 — 'B cannot exceed A by more than $k$' (with $x = A$, $y = B$):
It does NOT mean $y \le k$.
Trap 2 — 'A is at least twice B':
And 'B at most one-third of A' → $y \le \tfrac{1}{3}x$, that is $3y \le x$.

segments.text: Let me pin down the exact symbols, especially the two phrasings that trap students every year. Treat this as your translation reference.
First, the skeleton every model shares.
You write maximise or minimise Z equals a x plus b y, subject to the structural constraints, and then, always, x and y greater than or equal to zero.
Now trap one, the difference constraint. The sentence, B cannot exceed A by more than k, where x is A and y is B.
The correct translation is y minus x less than or equal to k, which you tidy up as minus x plus y less than or equal to k.
The mistake to avoid is huge here. It does not mean y less than or equal to k. The constraint is about the gap between the two variables, not a cap on y alone.
Trap two, the multiple constraint. The sentence, A is at least twice B.
This becomes x greater than or equal to two y, or equivalently x minus two y greater than or equal to zero. Read the direction carefully, because twice multiplies the smaller quantity.
And a common cousin, B is at most one-third of A, becomes y less than or equal to one-third x, which clears to three y less than or equal to x.
आइए exact symbols पक्के कर लें, ख़ासकर वो दो phrasings जो हर साल students को फँसाती हैं। इसे अपना translation reference समझिए।
पहले, वो skeleton जो हर model में common है।
आप लिखते हैं maximise या minimise Z equals a x plus b y, subject to structural constraints, और फिर, हमेशा, x और y greater than or equal to zero।
अब trap one, difference constraint। वाक्य, B, A से k से ज़्यादा नहीं बढ़ सकता, जहाँ x है A और y है B।
सही translation है y minus x less than or equal to k, जिसे साफ़ करके लिखते हैं minus x plus y less than or equal to k।
यहाँ बचने वाली ग़लती बड़ी है। इसका मतलब y less than or equal to k नहीं है। constraint दोनों variables के बीच के gap के बारे में है, अकेले y पर cap नहीं।
trap two, multiple constraint। वाक्य, A, B का कम से कम दोगुना है।
यह बनता है x greater than or equal to two y, या समान रूप से x minus two y greater than or equal to zero। direction ध्यान से पढ़िए, क्योंकि twice छोटी quantity को multiply करता है।
और एक common cousin, B, A का ज़्यादा से ज़्यादा one-third है, बनता है y less than or equal to one-third x, जो साफ़ होकर three y less than or equal to x।

segments.text: Let us run the full five steps on a product-mix problem that hides a difference constraint. A printing press makes cartons of ruled notebooks and cartons of sketchbooks.
Each carton of notebooks needs one unit of paper. Each carton of sketchbooks needs two units, because the pages are thicker. Let x be notebook cartons and y sketchbook cartons.
The press has one hundred units of paper, can finish at most seventy cartons in total per day, and, because demand is limited, sketchbook cartons cannot exceed notebook cartons by more than twenty.
Profit is sixty rupees per notebook carton and one hundred forty rupees per sketchbook carton.
So the objective is maximise Z equals sixty x plus one hundred forty y.

Translating clause by clause, paper gives x plus two y less than or equal to one hundred, total output gives x plus y less than or equal to seventy, and the difference clause gives minus x plus y less than or equal to twenty, with both variables non-negative.
Plot all three lines and shade the feasible region. It is the five-cornered polygon you see on the board.

Evaluate Z at every corner. Zero comma zero gives zero, seventy comma zero gives four thousand two hundred, forty comma thirty gives six thousand six hundred, twenty comma forty gives six thousand eight hundred, and zero comma twenty gives two thousand eight hundred.

The maximum is six thousand eight hundred at twenty comma forty. Notice the winning point sits exactly where the difference clause, minus x plus y equals twenty, is active. That is the very clause a careless reader would have dropped.
आइए एक product-mix problem पर पूरे पाँच steps चलाएँ जिसमें एक difference constraint छिपा है। एक printing press ruled notebooks और sketchbooks के cartons बनाती है।
notebooks के हर carton को एक unit paper चाहिए। sketchbooks के हर carton को दो units, क्योंकि pages मोटे हैं। माना x है notebook cartons और y है sketchbook cartons।
press के पास सौ units paper हैं, रोज़ ज़्यादा से ज़्यादा सत्तर cartons बना सकती है, और, demand limited होने से, sketchbook cartons, notebook cartons से बीस से ज़्यादा नहीं बढ़ सकते।
profit है साठ rupees per notebook carton और एक सौ चालीस rupees per sketchbook carton।
तो objective है maximise Z equals साठ x plus एक सौ चालीस y।

clause by clause translate करें, paper देता है x plus two y less than or equal to one hundred, total output देता है x plus y less than or equal to seventy, और difference clause देता है minus x plus y less than or equal to twenty, दोनों variables non-negative के साथ।
तीनों lines plot करें और feasible region shade करें। यह वो पाँच-corner वाला polygon है जो board पर है।

Z को हर corner पर evaluate करें। zero comma zero देता है zero, seventy comma zero देता है four thousand two hundred, forty comma thirty देता है six thousand six hundred, twenty comma forty देता है six thousand eight hundred, और zero comma twenty देता है two thousand eight hundred।

maximum है six thousand eight hundred, twenty comma forty पर। ग़ौर कीजिए winning point ठीक वहाँ है जहाँ difference clause, minus x plus y equals twenty, active है। यही वो clause है जिसे लापरवाह पढ़ने वाला छोड़ देता।

board_events.text: At (6, 6) all three constraints are equalities — land, labour and water are fully used.
Maximum profit ₹54,000: plant 6 hectares of wheat and 6 of mustard.

segments.text: Now a higher-order allocation problem where three constraints all bite at once. A farmer has twelve hectares to split between wheat and mustard.
Let x be hectares of wheat and y hectares of mustard. The land itself is capped at twelve hectares.

Wheat needs two person-days of labour per hectare, mustard needs one, and only eighteen are available. Wheat needs one unit of water per hectare, mustard needs three, and only twenty four are available.
Expected profit is five thousand rupees per hectare of wheat and four thousand per hectare of mustard, so we maximise Z equals five thousand x plus four thousand y.

The three limits become x plus y less than or equal to twelve for land, two x plus y less than or equal to eighteen for labour, and x plus three y less than or equal to twenty four for water, with both variables non-negative.
Plot the three lines. Something special happens here, which the board makes clear. All three lines pass through one single vertex.
Evaluate the corners. Zero comma zero gives zero, nine comma zero gives forty five thousand, six comma six gives fifty four thousand, and zero comma eight gives thirty two thousand.

The twist is at six comma six. There, all three constraints hold as equalities. Land is six plus six, that is twelve. Labour is twelve plus six, that is eighteen. Water is six plus eighteen, that is twenty four. Every resource is fully used.

So the maximum profit is fifty four thousand rupees. Plant six hectares of wheat and six of mustard. This is exactly why you must check every corner, because the winner is where the binding constraints intersect.
अब एक higher-order allocation problem जहाँ तीनों constraints एक साथ काम करती हैं। एक farmer के पास बारह hectares हैं wheat और mustard में बाँटने के लिए।
माना x है hectares of wheat और y है hectares of mustard। ज़मीन खुद बारह hectares पर capped है।
wheat को per hectare दो person-days labour चाहिए, mustard को एक, और सिर्फ़ अठारह available हैं। wheat को per hectare एक unit water, mustard को तीन, और सिर्फ़ चौबीस available।
expected profit है पाँच हज़ार rupees per hectare wheat और चार हज़ार per hectare mustard, तो हम maximise करते हैं Z equals पाँच हज़ार x plus चार हज़ार y।

तीनों limits बनती हैं x plus y less than or equal to twelve ज़मीन के लिए, two x plus y less than or equal to eighteen labour के लिए, और x plus three y less than or equal to twenty four water के लिए, दोनों variables non-negative के साथ।
तीनों lines plot कीजिए। यहाँ कुछ ख़ास होता है, जो board साफ़ दिखाता है। तीनों lines एक ही vertex से गुज़रती हैं।
corners evaluate कीजिए। zero comma zero देता है zero, nine comma zero देता है forty five thousand, six comma six देता है fifty four thousand, और zero comma eight देता है thirty two thousand।

twist है six comma six पर। वहाँ तीनों constraints equalities के तौर पर सही हैं। ज़मीन है छह plus छह, यानी बारह। labour है बारह plus छह, यानी अठारह। water है छह plus अठारह, यानी चौबीस। हर resource पूरा use हुआ।
तो maximum profit है fifty four thousand rupees। छह hectares wheat और छह mustard बोइए। यही वजह है कि हर corner check करना ज़रूरी है, क्योंकि winner वहाँ है जहाँ binding constraints काटती हैं।

segments.text: This one asks only for the model, which is perfect for drilling the diet family. A fitness coach blends two protein powders, P and Q, measured in scoops.
One scoop of P gives twelve grams of protein and twenty grams of carbohydrate. One scoop of Q gives eight grams of protein and thirty grams of carbohydrate. Let x be scoops of P and y scoops of Q.
The client needs at least forty eight grams of protein and at least one hundred twenty grams of carbohydrate per day. P costs fifteen rupees a scoop and Q costs ten.
Because this is a cost problem, the objective is minimise Z equals fifteen x plus ten y.
The protein requirement is twelve x plus eight y greater than or equal to forty eight, and dividing through by four tidies it to three x plus two y greater than or equal to twelve.
The carbohydrate requirement is twenty x plus thirty y greater than or equal to one hundred twenty, and dividing by ten gives two x plus three y greater than or equal to twelve.
Sketch the region. Because both constraints are greater-than-or-equal, the region sits above both lines and opens out to infinity. It is unbounded.

That is the whole point of recognising the family early. Diet means minimise, which means greater-than-or-equal constraints, which means an unbounded region, which means you must run the half-plane verification when you go on to solve.

The question asked for formulation only, so the model is complete. Minimise Z equals fifteen x plus ten y, subject to three x plus two y greater than or equal to twelve, two x plus three y greater than or equal to twelve, and both variables non-negative.
यह सिर्फ़ model माँगती है, जो diet family को पक्का करने के लिए perfect है। एक fitness coach दो protein powders मिलाता है, P और Q, scoops में।
P का एक scoop देता है बारह grams protein और बीस grams carbohydrate। Q का एक scoop देता है आठ grams protein और तीस grams carbohydrate। माना x है scoops of P और y है scoops of Q।
client को रोज़ कम से कम अड़तालीस grams protein और कम से कम एक सौ बीस grams carbohydrate चाहिए। P की cost पंद्रह rupees per scoop और Q की दस।
क्योंकि यह cost problem है, objective है minimise Z equals पंद्रह x plus दस y।
protein requirement है twelve x plus eight y greater than or equal to forty eight, और चार से भाग देने पर यह साफ़ होकर three x plus two y greater than or equal to twelve बनती है।
carbohydrate requirement है twenty x plus thirty y greater than or equal to one hundred twenty, और दस से भाग देने पर two x plus three y greater than or equal to twelve।
region बनाइए। क्योंकि दोनों constraints greater-than-or-equal हैं, region दोनों lines के ऊपर बैठता है और infinity तक खुलता है। यह unbounded है।
family को जल्दी पहचानने का यही पूरा मक़सद है। diet का मतलब minimise, यानी greater-than-or-equal constraints, यानी unbounded region, यानी solve करते समय आपको half-plane verification चलानी ही होगी।

सवाल ने सिर्फ़ formulation माँगा था, तो model पूरा है। minimise Z equals पंद्रह x plus दस y, subject to three x plus two y greater than or equal to twelve, two x plus three y greater than or equal to twelve, और दोनों variables non-negative।

board_events.text: Region is bounded (total capped at 20) ⇒ Theorem 2 gives both max and min at corners.
A mixed bag of 'at most / at least / capped at' becomes four clean lines — one per clause.

segments.text: Here is a pure translation drill with a mixed bag of phrasings. A student earns from two freelance gigs, data-entry and graphic design, in hours per week.
Let x be data-entry hours and y be graphic-design hours per week.
Clause one, she has at most twenty working hours a week. At most means less-than-or-equal, so x plus y less than or equal to twenty. This is a capacity constraint.
Clause two, her client caps data-entry at twelve hours. That is an upper bound on a single variable, x less than or equal to twelve.
Clause three, to build her portfolio she wants at least five hours of design. At least means greater-than-or-equal, so y greater than or equal to five. This is a requirement.
Data-entry pays one hundred fifty rupees an hour and design two hundred fifty, and she wants maximum earnings, so maximise Z equals one hundred fifty x plus two hundred fifty y.
Plot the four lines. Notice that y greater than or equal to five already forces y positive, so a separate y greater than or equal to zero is redundant but harmless.
The region is bounded, because the total-hours cap of twenty closes it off. So by Theorem two, both a maximum and a minimum exist at corner points, and it is ready for the graphical method.

The lesson is the payoff of clause-by-clause work. A single messy sentence full of at most, at least, and capped at becomes four clean lines, one per clause, once you translate each phrase separately.
यह एक शुद्ध translation drill है जिसमें कई तरह की phrasings मिली हैं। एक student दो freelance gigs से कमाता है, data-entry और graphic design, hours per week में।
माना x है data-entry hours और y है graphic-design hours per week।
clause one, उसके पास हफ़्ते में ज़्यादा से ज़्यादा बीस working hours हैं। at most का मतलब less-than-or-equal, तो x plus y less than or equal to twenty। यह एक capacity constraint है।
clause two, उसका client data-entry को बारह घंटे पर cap करता है। यह एक अकेले variable पर upper bound है, x less than or equal to twelve।
clause three, portfolio बनाने के लिए वो कम से कम पाँच घंटे design चाहती है। at least का मतलब greater-than-or-equal, तो y greater than or equal to five। यह एक requirement है।
data-entry एक सौ पचास rupees प्रति घंटा देती है और design दो सौ पचास, और वो maximum earnings चाहती है, तो maximise Z equals एक सौ पचास x plus दो सौ पचास y।
चारों lines plot कीजिए। ग़ौर कीजिए कि y greater than or equal to five पहले ही y को positive कर देता है, तो अलग से y greater than or equal to zero redundant है पर harmless।
region bounded है, क्योंकि total-hours का बीस वाला cap इसे बंद कर देता है। तो Theorem two से, maximum और minimum दोनों corner points पर exist करते हैं, और यह graphical method के लिए तैयार है।
सबक़ है clause-by-clause काम का फ़ायदा। at most, at least, और capped at से भरा एक गड़बड़ वाक्य चार साफ़ lines बन जाता है, हर clause के लिए एक, जब आप हर phrase अलग translate करते हैं।

sections.title: Formulation pitfalls and a ten-second sanity scan

board_events.text: Formulation pitfalls and a 10-second sanity scan
Pitfall 1 — reversing ≤ and ≥. 'At least' is ≥; 'at most' is ≤. Underline the limiting words first.
Pitfall 2 — dropping a hidden constraint. 'B cannot exceed A by more than 100' is a full constraint.
Work clause by clause so no restriction escapes.
Pitfall 3 — forgetting non-negativity. Examiners deduct marks for a missing $x \ge 0,\ y \ge 0$.
Pitfall 4 — wrong decision variables. If you can't write everything in $x, y$, re-read the question.
Sanity scan: (i) max/min matches the goal word? (ii) one constraint per limiting sentence?
(iii) is non-negativity present? (iv) do cost/'at least' carry ≥ and profit/'at most' carry ≤?

segments.text: Let me close Part two with the four formulation slips that cost marks, and a ten-second scan that catches almost all of them.

Pitfall one, reversing the inequality. At least is greater-than-or-equal, at most is less-than-or-equal. A single flip turns a sensible answer into nonsense, so underline the limiting words before writing any symbol.
Pitfall two, dropping a hidden constraint. Sentences like B cannot exceed A by more than one hundred, or must produce at least ten of B, are full constraints in disguise.
The cure is the same discipline as before. Work through the paragraph clause by clause, so not a single restriction escapes you.

Pitfall three, forgetting non-negativity. Items, hours, kilograms, hectares, none can be negative. Examiners deduct marks for a missing x and y greater than or equal to zero, even if everything else is perfect.

Pitfall four, choosing the wrong decision variables. If you cannot write the objective and every constraint using just your two variables, you picked them badly. Re-read the question and take whatever it asks you to decide.
And here is the ten-second sanity scan to run after every formulation. First, does the objective say max or min to match the goal word? Second, is there one constraint for each limiting sentence?

Third, is non-negativity present? And fourth, do the cost and at-least problems carry greater-than-or-equal, while the profit and at-most problems carry less-than-or-equal? If all four check out, your model is almost certainly right.
Part two को उन चार formulation slips से बंद करते हैं जो marks खर्च कराती हैं, और एक दस-second scan से जो इनमें से लगभग सब पकड़ लेती है।

pitfall one, inequality उलट देना। at least है greater-than-or-equal, at most है less-than-or-equal। एक flip समझदार answer को बकवास बना देता है, तो कोई symbol लिखने से पहले limiting words underline कीजिए।
pitfall two, hidden constraint छोड़ देना। वाक्य जैसे B, A से सौ से ज़्यादा नहीं बढ़ सकता, या कम से कम दस B बनाने ही हैं, ये छुपे हुए पूरे constraints हैं।
इलाज वही discipline है। paragraph को clause by clause पढ़िए, ताकि एक भी restriction आपसे ना छूटे।

pitfall three, non-negativity भूल जाना। items, hours, kilograms, hectares, कोई भी negative नहीं हो सकता। examiners छूटे हुए x और y greater than or equal to zero के लिए marks काटते हैं, चाहे बाकी सब perfect हो।

pitfall four, ग़लत decision variables चुनना। अगर आप objective और हर constraint को सिर्फ़ अपने दो variables में नहीं लिख सकते, तो आपने ग़लत चुने। सवाल दोबारा पढ़िए और वही लीजिए जो वो decide करने को कहता है।
और यह रहा हर formulation के बाद चलाने वाला दस-second sanity scan। पहला, क्या objective max या min goal word से match करता है? दूसरा, क्या हर limiting sentence के लिए एक constraint है?

तीसरा, क्या non-negativity मौजूद है? और चौथा, क्या cost और at-least problems में greater-than-or-equal है, जबकि profit और at-most problems में less-than-or-equal? अगर चारों सही हैं, तो आपका model लगभग ज़रूर सही है।

sections.title: The four possible outcomes of an LPP

board_events.text: Four ways a Linear Programming problem can end
So far every LPP behaved nicely: one region, one clean optimal corner. Real problems don't always cooperate.
1. One clear highest spot — a unique optimal solution (the usual, happy case).
2. A whole ridge at the same height — multiple optimal solutions.
3. The field never ends uphill — an unbounded solution; no highest point exists.
4. There is no field at all — no feasible solution; the constraints contradict.

board_events.text: Infeasible: 'sell at least 60' but 'shelf holds at most 40' — no honest number works.

segments.text: Until now every problem we solved behaved beautifully. One feasible region, one clean optimal corner. But real problems, and exam problems designed to test you, do not always cooperate.
Think of solving an L P P as searching a fenced field for the highest point your ruler reads. Exactly four things can happen, and a complete student recognises all four on sight.
Outcome one, there is one clear highest spot. This is the unique optimal solution, the usual, happy case we have seen all along.
Outcome two, there is a whole ridge at the same height. Your ruler lies flat along one fence, so every point on that fence ties for best. These are multiple optimal solutions.
Outcome three, the field never ends in the uphill direction. You can keep walking and keep climbing forever, so there is no highest point. That is an unbounded solution.
Outcome four, there is no field at all. The fences contradict each other so badly that no point satisfies them all. The region is empty, and the problem has no answer.
The board shows all four side by side. Learn to picture each one, because naming the outcome quickly is the whole skill of this subtopic.

Here is the vivid version of outcome four. A shopkeeper insists, I must sell at least sixty items today, but also, my shelf holds at most forty items. No honest number can satisfy both. That is an infeasible problem.
अब तक हमने जो भी problem solve की वो बहुत अच्छे से behave करती रही। एक feasible region, एक साफ़ optimal corner। लेकिन असली problems, और आपको test करने वाली exam problems, हमेशा cooperate नहीं करतीं।
एक L P P को solve करना ऐसे सोचिए जैसे एक बाड़ वाले field में सबसे ऊँचा point ढूँढना जहाँ आपका ruler पढ़ता है। ठीक चार चीज़ें हो सकती हैं, और एक पूरा student चारों को देखते ही पहचान लेता है।
outcome one, एक साफ़ सबसे ऊँचा spot है। यह unique optimal solution है, वही आम, ख़ुशगवार case जो हम अब तक देखते आए हैं।
outcome two, एक ही ऊँचाई पर पूरी ridge है। आपका ruler एक बाड़ के साथ सपाट लेट जाता है, तो उस बाड़ का हर point best के लिए tie करता है। ये multiple optimal solutions हैं।
outcome three, field uphill direction में कभी ख़त्म नहीं होता। आप चलते रह सकते हैं और चढ़ते रह सकते हैं, तो कोई सबसे ऊँचा point है ही नहीं। यह unbounded solution है।
outcome four, field है ही नहीं। बाड़ें एक दूसरे को इतना contradict करती हैं कि कोई point सबको satisfy नहीं करता। region खाली है, और problem का कोई answer नहीं।
board चारों को साथ-साथ दिखाता है। हर एक को picture करना सीखिए, क्योंकि outcome को जल्दी नाम देना ही इस subtopic का पूरा skill है।
